title: Static electricity (physics only)
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Static electricity (physics only) — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.2.5.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Static electricity (physics only), specification section 4.2.5.
final_note: You worked through Static electricity (physics only) — 12 specification statements.

concepts.def: Electric charge that has built up on an object and stays where it is, rather than flowing as a current. It is produced when certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other.
When certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other they become electrically charged: negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
The movement of electrons from one object to another. Only electrons move when objects are rubbed; the positively charged nuclei stay fixed in place in the material.
An object that has gained electrons. The material that gains electrons in rubbing becomes negatively charged.
An object that has lost electrons. The material that loses electrons is left with a positive charge, because it now has more positive charge in its nuclei than negative charge in its electrons.
The material that loses electrons is left with a charge equal in size to the negative charge on the material that gains them, because every electron gained by one is an electron lost by the other.
A material that charge cannot flow through. Charge produced by rubbing stays on the surface of an insulator instead of flowing away, which is why static charge can build up on it.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel: two negatively charged objects push each other apart, and so do two positively charged objects.
Two objects that carry different types of charge attract: a positively charged object and a negatively charged object pull each other together.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between two charged objects are examples of non-contact force.

As charge builds up on an object by rubbing, the potential difference between it and a nearby earthed object grows. When it is large enough, charge moves across the gap through the air, and this sudden movement of charge is seen and heard as a spark.

concepts.term: Ionisation of the air in a spark
concepts.def: When the electric field in the gap becomes strong enough, it pulls electrons off atoms in the air. The air then contains charged particles that are free to move, so it can conduct, and charge flows across the gap as a spark.
The region around a charged object in which another charged object experiences a force. A charged object creates an electric field around itself.
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object, and the further away from the charged object, the weaker the field.

concepts.term: Electric field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
concepts.def: Straight lines drawn from the surface of the sphere, spreading out evenly in all directions. The arrows point away from a positively charged sphere and towards a negatively charged sphere. The lines are closest together near the surface, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart with distance, where the field is weaker.

concepts.term: Force on a second charged object
concepts.def: A second charged object placed in the field of a charged object experiences a force. The force gets stronger as the distance between the objects decreases.

concepts.term: Field explanation of a non-contact force
concepts.def: Each charged object creates a field around itself, and the other object sits inside that field. The force acts on each object because of the field at its own position, so the objects do not need to touch for a force to act.

concepts.term: Suspended rod test (evidence for electrostatic forces)
concepts.def: A charged rod is hung on a thread so that it can turn freely. A second charged rod brought near it, without touching, makes it turn away if the two carry the same type of charge and turn towards if they carry different types. This is evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when not in contact.

mcqs.q: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?
options: Rubbing creates new charge on the surfaces of both of the materials.
Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.
Electrons are rubbed off both materials and lost into the air nearby.
Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other material.
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification states: negatively charged electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, leaving one negatively charged and one positively charged.

mcqs.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What is the charge on the cloth?
options: A smaller positive charge, because the cloth keeps most of its electrons.
An equal positive charge, because the cloth lost electrons to the rod.
An equal positive charge, because protons moved from the rod to the cloth.
No charge at all, because the charge was created on the rod by rubbing.
mcqs.explain: The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged and the material that loses them is left with an equal positive charge.

mcqs.q: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material equal in size to the negative charge on the other?
options: Because rubbing makes equal amounts of new positive and negative charge.
Because charge made by rubbing spreads out evenly between the materials.
Because equal numbers of protons and electrons move in opposite directions.
Because every electron gained by one material is one lost by the other.
mcqs.explain: The charges are equal because they arise from the same transfer: the surplus of electrons on one material exactly matches the shortfall on the other.

mcqs.q: A student rubs a metal rod held in her hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?
options: Charge flows through the metal and her body, so none stays on the rod.
Metals are unable to gain or lose any electrons when they are rubbed.
The cloth becomes charged as well, so the two charges cancel each other.
The charge spreads over the whole rod, so it becomes too weak to detect.
mcqs.explain: Static charge builds up only on insulating materials. A metal conducts, so charge transferred by rubbing flows away to earth through the hand.

mcqs.q: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?
options: Objects with the same type of charge attract; different types repel.
The objects only push or pull once their surfaces are touching.
Objects with the same type of charge repel; different types attract.
The objects attract each other, whatever charges they carry.
mcqs.explain: Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel, and two objects that carry different types of charge attract.

mcqs.q: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same cloth. One is hung on a thread and the other is brought near it. What happens, and why?
options: It swings towards it, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
It stays still, because the two rods are not yet touching each other.
It swings away, because both rods carry the same type of charge.
It swings away, because the rods carry different types of charge.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing identical rods with the same cloth gives both the same type of charge, and two objects carrying the same type of charge repel.

mcqs.q: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when not in contact?
options: Two charged rods push each other apart when their ends are touching.
A rubbed rod feels warm to the touch after it has been rubbed hard.
A suspended charged rod turns away as a second charged rod nears it.
A magnet attracts a steel pin without the two objects ever touching.
mcqs.explain: The suspended rod moves while a gap remains, so a force is acting between two charged objects that are not in contact.

mcqs.q: A charged polythene rod repels another charged polythene rod. A student says this shows the rods are magnetic. Which response is correct?
options: No - the rods repel because both carry the same type of charge.
Yes - repulsion across a gap can only happen between magnetic poles.
Yes - rubbing a plastic rod turns it into a weak permanent magnet.
No - but the rods must carry different types of charge to repel.
mcqs.explain: Both rods were charged the same way, so they carry the same type of charge and repel. This is an electrostatic force, not magnetism.

mcqs.q: A student walks across a nylon carpet and gets a small shock as her hand approaches a metal door handle. Why?
options: Positive charges jump from the metal handle across the gap to her hand.
Air cannot conduct, so the shock comes from friction heating her skin.
Rubbing has charged the student, and charge moves across the small gap.
Walking creates new charge, which the metal handle then destroys again.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the student; the charge then crosses the gap to the earthed handle, which is the spark she feels.

mcqs.q: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps to a nearby earthed metal object. Which explanation is correct?
options: The field becomes strong enough to pull electrons off atoms in the air.
Air always insulates, so the charge must travel along a damp surface.
Protons move across the gap from the object to the earthed metal.
The field is weakest at the surface, so charge escapes from there first.
mcqs.explain: The field in the gap grows as charge builds up; once it is strong enough it ionises the air, the air conducts, and charge crosses the gap as a spark.

mcqs.q: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth. Both become positively charged. Which explanation in terms of electrons is correct?
options: Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the two rods now repel.
Rubbing made new positive charge on each rod, which the cloths took.
Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the two rods now attract.
mcqs.explain: Losing electrons leaves each rod positively charged, and two objects carrying the same type of charge repel each other.

options: The path a charged object follows when it is released near a charge.
The lines on the surface of a charged object along which charge sits.
The stream of electrons that flows away from a charged object.
The region round a charged object where another charge feels a force.
mcqs.explain: A charged object creates an electric field around itself, and a second charged object placed in that field experiences a force.

mcqs.q: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change with distance from the sphere?
options: It is weakest close to the sphere and gets stronger further away.
It has the same strength everywhere until the field lines end.
It is strongest at a fixed distance out from the sphere's surface.
It is strongest close to the sphere and gets weaker further away.
mcqs.explain: The electric field is strongest close to the charged object, and the further away from it, the weaker the field.

mcqs.q: A charged sphere is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force on the second object?
options: It gets weaker, because the field is stronger further from the sphere.
It gets stronger, because the field is stronger nearer the sphere.
It stays the same, because the charge on the sphere has not changed.
It stays at zero, because the two objects are still not touching.
mcqs.explain: The field is strongest close to the charged object, so the force on a second charged object gets stronger as the distance decreases.

mcqs.q: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated positively charged sphere?
options: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, with arrows going clockwise.
Straight lines spreading out all round the sphere, with arrows pointing out.
Parallel lines spaced evenly across the sphere, with arrows pointing up.
Straight lines spreading out all round the sphere, with arrows pointing in.
mcqs.explain: The field of an isolated charged sphere is radial. The arrows point away from a positively charged sphere, and the lines are closest together at the surface.

mcqs.q: In the field diagram for a charged sphere, why are the field lines drawn closer together near the surface?
options: Because the field is stronger there than it is further from the sphere.
Because charge can only be found where the lines have been drawn in.
Because a charged object placed there would travel along those lines.
Because the lines must meet at the surface, where the field ends.
mcqs.explain: Spacing shows field strength: the lines are closest where the field is strongest, which is close to the charged object.

mcqs.q: A student says there is no field in the gaps between the field lines on a diagram. Which response is correct?
options: Right - the field only exists along the lines that have been drawn on.
Right - the lines show the only paths that a charge is able to follow.
Wrong - but the field is only found beyond the last line on the page.
Wrong - the field fills the space, and the lines are a way of showing it.
mcqs.explain: The number of lines drawn is a choice; the field exists throughout the region around the charged object, and the spacing of the lines shows its strength.

mcqs.q: How does the idea of an electric field explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?
options: Each object sits in the other's field, so each one experiences a force.
The two fields must meet and touch before either object feels a force.
Each field reaches out a fixed distance, and beyond that there is none.
One object pushes on the air, and the air then pushes the other object.
mcqs.explain: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed in that field experiences a force, so no contact is needed.
